# The Jevons paradox of decisions {#sec-ch12}

::: {.epigraph by="Roy Amara, attributed"}
We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run.
:::

In 1865 the economist William Stanley Jevons noticed something odd about coal [@jevons1865]. James Watt's steam engine got far more work from each ton than older engines. Surely Britain would now burn *less* coal? It burned far more. Cheaper coal-powered work got used for more things, in more mills, mines and railways. Each engine used less; the country used more.

Jev's name is short for Jevons. So what's the coal this time? Decisions.

![The pattern Jevons saw in coal, and the same pattern with decisions. Making each unit cheaper opens up uses that weren't worth it before, and total use can rise.](/figures/ch19/loop.pdf){#fig-loop-12}

::: {.goals}
- Explain when making something cheaper makes us use more of it.
- Work out when a decision is worth making at all, from its value, price and deadline.
- See where the paradox really shows up: in new jobs, not old ones.
- Notice the hidden cost: cheap decisions move work onto the people who review them.
:::

## Cheaper things get used for more things

When a photo meant buying film and paying for prints, you took a few dozen on holiday. Now each costs nothing, and you take thousands: receipts, parking spots, whiteboards. When light got cheap, from candles to LEDs, people didn't keep the savings; they lit streets all night [@fouquet2006]. That's the **Jevons paradox**: each unit gets cheaper, and total use rises.

It isn't a law. Salt is cheap, but nobody eats ten times as much. It depends on how much new demand a lower price unlocks. So the real question is: *are there many decisions nobody makes today, only because they cost too much?*

## When is a decision worth making?

Every decision has a **value**: the expected loss it avoids. If an alert has a 3% chance of being a \$10,000 break-in that a good decision would stop, checking it is worth about \$300. A decision is worth making when its value is above its price.

A company makes a few thousand careful decisions a day. But it *could* make millions: every incoming email, every login, every line in the logs. Each is almost certainly fine, so each is worth checking only if the check costs a tiny fraction of a cent.

![A simple, illustrative model of a company's decision pools. Each line spans the middle 90% of decision values in a pool, with the median as a dot. A decision is worth making when its value is to the right of its price. At the LLM price, most emails, logins and log lines aren't worth asking about. At Jev's vendor-reported price, most are.](/figures/ch19/pools.pdf){#fig-pools}

@fig-pools is a deliberately simple model; every number in it is an assumption. A typical log line is worth about two thousandths of a cent to check. At this book's illustrative LLM price of \${{< num ch19 llm_price f5 >}} a decision, almost none are worth it. At Jev's vendor-reported price of \${{< num ch19 jev_price f6 >}}, about half are.

Price isn't the only gate. **Time** is the other. A person logging in will wait a few hundred milliseconds before the delay itself becomes the problem; an email can wait seconds; an alert, a minute. A decision gets made only if it's cheap enough *and* fast enough (@fig-gates).

![A decision gets made only if it's cheap enough (value above price) and fast enough (answer inside the time budget). The shaded regions show which decisions each option can make, using this book's illustrative LLM figures and Jev's vendor-reported price and latency range. Logins fall inside Jev's region only at the fast end of that range.](/figures/ch19/gates.pdf){#fig-gates}

::: {.keyidea}
A decision is worth making only when it's cheaper than the loss it avoids and faster than its deadline.
:::

## Where the paradox shows up

With both gates applied, the illustrative LLM makes about {{< num ch19 llm_decisions approx >}} decisions a day for about \${{< num ch19 llm_spend int >}}. A Jev-priced model makes about {{< num ch19 jev_decisions approx >}} for about \${{< num ch19 jev_spend int >}}: {{< num ch19 decisions_ratio int >}} times the decisions for a quarter of the bill.

So inside the jobs a company already does, the bill goes *down*. The newly affordable decisions are each worth so little that, together, they avoid only about \${{< num ch19 value_gain int >}} of losses a day.

The paradox appears in jobs that don't exist yet. Suppose cheap decisions make a new job worth building: checking every file shared outside the company, {{< num ch19 new_job approx >}} a day, each worth a few thousandths of a cent. At LLM prices nobody would build it. At Jev's price the model makes about {{< num ch19 jev_new_taken approx >}} of those checks a day, and the decision bill jumps to about \${{< num ch19 jev_new_spend int >}}. Add a few jobs like that and the company spends more on decisions than ever, while making dozens of times as many. That's Jevons' coal again.

::: {.keyidea}
Cheaper decisions rarely raise the bill for jobs you already do; they raise it by making new jobs worth doing.
:::

## The hidden cost: where the work goes

The result I'd most want you to take to work: more decisions means more cases that end with a person.

![Alerts sent to a person per day, under two rules (illustrative). A rule that flags a fixed share of what the model looks at grows with the number of decisions, and at Jev volumes it sends far more than the team can handle. A cost-based threshold, which flags only when the expected loss is larger than the cost of a review, barely moves.](/figures/ch19/flags.pdf){#fig-flags}

Keep a rule that seemed sensible at low volume, "send the top 0.1% to a person", and it sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_llm int >}} a day, comfortably under the team's capacity of {{< num ch19 capacity int >}}. At Jev volumes the same rule sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_jev int >}} (@fig-flags). Nobody changed the policy; the queue just grew eightfold. A cost-based threshold, which flags a case only when its expected loss beats the \$15 a review costs, sends {{< num ch19 flags_cost_jev int >}} a day either way.

::: {.keyidea}
When decisions get cheap, set thresholds by cost, not by share.
:::

And calibration matters *more* as decisions multiply. An overconfident model making a million decisions a day doesn't make a few extra mistakes; it fills the queue.

::: {.breaks}
Everything in this chapter's model is an assumption: the pools, their sizes, the value of each decision, the time limits. Change them and the numbers move a lot. Jev's price and latency are vendor-reported and may change. History offers hints, not proof: only the next few years will show whether demand for decisions behaves like light or like salt.
:::

::: {.threshold}
A company wants to check every login as it happens: 150,000 a day, each check worth about \$0.0005, with a 300-millisecond limit. At Jev's vendor-reported price, is it worth it? What would you measure first?

(At \$0.000021 a check, yes: a typical login is worth about twenty times its check. The open question is time. Measure latency from your own network at your own volumes, including the slowest calls. And send a login to a person only when its expected loss beats the cost of a review, never as a fixed share.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Name something in your life that got much cheaper. Do you use the same, more, or more *and* spend more in total?
2. Write down a rule from your own work that's set as a share ("the top 5%") rather than a cost. What happens to it if volume grows tenfold?
:::
